function.name: data_access
function.description:
The warehouse (`atlas_prod`) — discover, query, and load data. One tool,
    several actions. (The user's OWN uploaded files are separate: use `user_data`.)

    SQL — raw read-only query; the escape hatch for ad-hoc/exploratory work,
    joins, counts, and non-series tables:
      data_access(action="sql", query="SELECT ...")   (optional save_as + description to cache)

    DISCOVER — "what data do we have / what can I forecast": the CURATED catalog
    (described entries + sample_queries) — the best starting point. With `query`,
    runs an econ-series name search instead — a NARROW search, so never conclude
    data is absent from a query miss:
      data_access(action="discover")                  curated catalog
      data_access(action="discover", query="cheese")  econ-series name search

    SCHEMAS — the LIVE inventory of everything the agent can actually read (the
    access allowlist), straight from the database. Use it when discover comes up
    empty — it surfaces data that exists but isn't catalogued yet:
      data_access(action="schemas")                        schema → table map
      data_access(action="schemas", target_schema="usda_raw")  tables + columns

    LOAD — the canonical loader for ONE OR MANY series. Resolves each series_id →
    pd.Series w/ DatetimeIndex, saved as its OWN discrete stash entry (own index),
    optionally tagged with a `group`. Returns a SINGLE-SHAPE reference (no raw values):
    `{group, loaded:[{stash_name,series_id,name,rows,range}], missing:[{series_id,reason}]}`.
    Use this for a set of series — do NOT iterate load_series then merge into one panel
    (different spans → a null-riddled frame). Each series stays discrete; align downstream
    only if you must (`pd.DataFrame({...})`):
      data_access(action="load", series_ids=["...","..."], group="treasury_yields")

    LOAD_SERIES — single-series shortcut (same discrete save, series-stats reference).
    Do NOT hand-write SQL against data.regressors; the resolution is brittle:
      data_access(action="load_series", series_id="...", start_date="...", stash_name="...")

    QUERY_DATA — per-series summary statistics (count, missing %, date range,
    mean/min/max) for known series_ids — NOT the raw observations (use
    load_series to get the actual values):
      data_access(action="query_data", series_ids=["..."], start_date="...", end_date="...")

    BROWSE / GET_DETAIL — catalog navigation: `browse` lists distinct values of a
    field (commodity/source_schema/unit); `get_detail` shows one series' metadata.
    HELP — `data_access(action="help")` lists available actions.

    Args:
        action: sql | discover | schemas | load | load_series | query_data | browse | get_detail | help
        query: SQL for action="sql"; econ-series search term for action="discover"
        series_ids: series_ids for action="load" (multi-series load) and query_data (summary stats)
        series_id: single series_id for load_series / get_detail
        group: optional batch label for action="load" — ties the discrete series saved together
        start_date / end_date: date filters for query_data / load_series (YYYY-MM-DD)
        field: column to browse — commodity, source_schema, unit
        limit: max results
        stash_name: optional stash key for load_series (default: slug of series name)
        target_schema: schema filter — for discover (one catalog area) or schemas (drill into one schema's tables+columns)
        save_as: optional stash key to cache an action="sql" result DataFrame
        description: required with save_as — describes the cached data

function.name: user_data
function.description:
The user's OWN uploaded datasets — private per-customer SQL tables,
    SEPARATE from the shared warehouse — one tool, two actions.

    LIST (default) — names, columns, row counts of their uploaded datasets:
      user_data(action="list")
    QUERY — read-only DuckDB SQL over those datasets (JOIN-able with each
    other; cannot reach the warehouse — use data_access(action="sql") for that).
    Returns a capped PREVIEW (up to 50 rows; truncated at 10,000) — for full
    data, pull it in execute_code via query_my_data(...):
      user_data(action="query", sql="SELECT ... FROM <table>")

function.name: execute_code
function.description:
Execute Python code in a Jupyter kernel sandbox.

    The sandbox is pre-configured with imports and helpers specific
    to the current agent. See the system prompt for available
    libraries, functions, and stash operations.

    Persistence (IMPORTANT): variables persist within a turn and USUALLY across
    turns, but the kernel can be EVICTED between turns (idle timeout or capacity)
    — which wipes every variable, model, and import. Do NOT assume a variable
    from a previous turn still exists. Call namespace.variables() to check what's
    actually in scope; save anything you must keep across turns to the stash (it
    survives eviction, the kernel may not); use code_recall to rebuild prior work.

    Plotting: every `plotly.graph_objects.Figure` (including those returned
    by plotly.express) auto-renders to the user's chat panel at end of cell —
    do NOT call `fig.show()`, `display(fig)`, or leave `fig` as the cell's
    last expression. The tool result's `figures` field is always `[]` after
    plots are sent (they go via a side channel); the stdout line
    `[N plot(s) sent to chat — visible to the user]` confirms success.
    Calling `.show()` on top of auto-render produces duplicate plots and
    is the single most common plotting mistake — just create the figure
    and let the cell end. matplotlib / seaborn do NOT reach the user's
    card — use plotly.

    Tables: `display_dataframe(df, title="...")` ships a DataFrame to the
    user's table card (scrollable, up to 5000 rows) — the table
    equivalent of letting a Figure auto-render. Use it whenever the user
    needs to see more than ~30 rows; for ≤30 rows prefer a markdown table in
    your reply. The stdout line `[N table(s) sent to chat — visible to the
    user]` confirms success. After calling it, summarize in your reply what
    was sent (key columns, notable rows) — the user sees the card, not your
    stdout.

    Loading SOURCE data (the warehouse + the user's uploads) is GATED per agent.
    The in-kernel loaders you actually have — if any — are listed in your system
    prompt under "## Loading source data"; use those to pull FULL results straight
    into a variable (the `data_access` sql tool only returns a capped preview). Do
    NOT guess a loader name: if your prompt doesn't list one, it is NOT defined in
    your kernel (calling it fails lint), and you do not load source data yourself —
    read what the data_load sub already assembled from the stash instead:
    `df = stash.load("<handle>")` (see the `## Stash` block for handles).

    Your analytical toolbox: `libs()` prints the modeling libraries available to
    you in this kernel, grouped by purpose (installed-only, so it never lies) —
    call it before reaching for a library so you use one you actually have.
    `libs("forecast")` filters to matching groups. For HOW to use a library, ask
    the code_info sub (docs + worked examples).

    Inspect your namespace with the `namespace` object (persists with the kernel):
    namespace.variables() lists live data variables (name + type/shape),
    namespace.variables(detail=True) adds DataFrame previews, namespace.functions()
    lists functions you defined in earlier cells (signature + docstring), and
    namespace.source("name") prints a defined function's source. variables()/
    functions() accept an optional name filter, e.g. namespace.variables("df"), and
    print a readable summary AND return a list of {name, type, shape, ...} dicts you
    can capture and slice: v = namespace.variables(); v[:5]. Use these instead of
    re-printing things to see what's in scope.

    Leave yourself breadcrumbs on a long-lived kernel — they survive context
    compaction, so a later you knows what a name was for: DOCSTRING your helper
    functions (namespace.functions() shows the docstring back), and for the small
    odds-and-ends that aren't worth stashing (a threshold, a fitted scalar, a derived
    index) call namespace.note("thr", "decision threshold from the ROC knee") —
    namespace.variables() then shows the note inline. The stash is for the big
    described artifacts (panels, models, result series); notes are for everything
    smaller. Notes are best-effort across kernel eviction — stash what MUST survive.

    Commenting: comment generously and make every cell self-contained and
    self-explanatory. State the PURPOSE of the analysis, your APPROACH, and key
    assumptions/decisions — not just what a line does. Your comments are what
    `code_recall` matches on for semantic search AND the only context a future
    session gets when it pulls this code back up: code recalled with no comments
    is useless. Good comments now = findable later + understandable on reuse.

    Annotate outcomes — don't skip this. When a cell settles a unit of work,
    before moving on, record the verdict on it: a clean, reusable result →
    code_recall(action="note", id="<this run>", verdict="good", note="<why>");
    a failure or dead end → verdict="dead_end" with the reason (this is what
    stops a future session from re-running the same broken approach). Back-fill
    the verdict on an EARLIER run once a later cell proves it worked or failed.
    Verdicts are not optional bookkeeping — they are what makes recall rank the
    good code first and surface the lesson behind the bad. For a result you'd
    want to reuse months from now, `code_recall(action="promote", id=...)` it.

    Args:
        code: Python code to execute.

function.name: stash
function.description:
Session blackboard for data artifacts across turns — one tool, five actions.

    NOTE: for Python objects (models, fitted pipelines, large DataFrames, numpy
    arrays) DO NOT use this tool — call `stash.save(name, obj, description,
    kind=..., inputs=[...])` INSIDE execute_code (the in-kernel stash pickles
    objects directly). This tool is only for small JSON-encodable
    config/lists/primitives.

    LIST (default) — what's saved this session (check before reloading data):
      stash(action="list")
    LOAD — fetch a saved item by name (DataFrames show shape/columns/head; other
    objects return a 500-char string preview):
      stash(action="load", name="y")
    SAVE — store small JSON data (typed metadata optional but preferred):
      stash(action="save", name="cfg", description="...", data_json="{...}", kind="config", inputs=["raw"])
      kind ∈ dataframe|model|plot|analysis|text|config; inputs = upstream entry names (for lineage).
    REMOVE — delete a saved item:
      stash(action="remove", name="y")
    LINEAGE — trace what an artifact was derived from (walks `inputs` back):
      stash(action="lineage", name="model")

function.name: compare
function.description:
Evaluate relationships between a target series and driver series.

    Args:
        target_id: The target series_id
        driver_ids: Driver series_ids (required for cross_correlation/correlation_matrix)
        method: cross_correlation | correlation_matrix | discover_correlates
            (call with method='help' for full details)
        max_lag: Maximum lag to test in weeks (default 26; positive lag = driver leads target)
        params: Extra parameters for discover_correlates
            (top_n, commodity, source_schema, transform, min_lag)

generations.text:
I searched the warehouse for U.S. natural gas consumption data with a longer historical range. 

The most relevant series found is **`natgas_total_consumption`**, which tracks the total natural gas delivered to consumers in the U.S. However, its available historical range in the warehouse only extends from **January 2001 to April 2026**, which does not meet your requirement for data going back to the 1980s.

Other related series (Commercial, Industrial, and Residential consumption) were also identified, but they share the same limited date range.

**Summary of findings:**

| Series ID | Description | Date Range | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `natgas_total_consumption` | Natural gas total delivered to consumers in the U.S. | 2001-01-07 to 2026-04-26 | mmcf |

No series matching your specific criteria (1980s or earlier) was found in the current warehouse catalog or the live `data.series_lookup` table.
